::: {.callout-note}
**Inference labs** use the five-step template:
Hypothesis → Visualise → Assumptions → Conduct → Conclude.
:::

## Learning objectives

- Fit a logistic regression with `glm(family = binomial)` and translate
  coefficients into odds ratios.
- Construct a confusion matrix at a chosen probability threshold.
- Report the model with an odds ratio, an interval, and a brief note on
  discrimination.

## Prerequisites

Week 1 regression material.

## Background

Logistic regression models the log-odds of a binary outcome as a
linear combination of predictors. The exponent of a coefficient is
the odds ratio for a one-unit increase in the corresponding predictor.
Because the relationship is linear on the log-odds scale and not the
probability scale, a slope of 0.5 log-odds is a larger change in
probability near 0.5 than near 0.95.

The model is fit by maximum likelihood with iteratively reweighted
least squares. Standard errors are computed from the observed
information, and Wald intervals on the log-odds scale are exponentiated
to give intervals on the odds ratio. Profile-likelihood intervals are
more trustworthy when the sample is small or the predictor is strongly
associated with the outcome.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
A confusion matrix at a single threshold tells only part of the story;
the thresholds used in the clinic may not be the one that maximises
accuracy. Week 3, Session 5 covers ROC curves and calibration, which
give a threshold-free view of the same model.
:::

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(MASS)
set.seed(42)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## 1. Hypothesis

Using `MASS::Pima.tr`, can plasma glucose (`glu`) predict diabetes
status (`type`)?

## 2. Visualise

```{r}
pima <- as_tibble(Pima.tr) |>
  mutate(type = factor(type, levels = c("No", "Yes")))

ggplot(pima, aes(type, glu, fill = type)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, colour = "grey30") +
  labs(x = "Diabetes", y = "Plasma glucose") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## 3. Assumptions

Binary outcome, independent observations, log-odds linear in the
predictors (or handled explicitly with a smooth/transformation).

```{r}
fit <- glm(type ~ glu, data = pima, family = binomial)
fit_spline <- glm(type ~ splines::ns(glu, df = 3), data = pima, family = binomial)
# Compare a flexible specification; plotting fitted logits from the linear
# model alone cannot check linearity, because they are linear by construction.
print(anova(fit, fit_spline, test = "LRT"))
binned <- pima |>
  mutate(y = as.integer(type == "Yes"), bin = ntile(glu, 8)) |>
  group_by(bin) |>
  summarise(glu = mean(glu), successes = sum(y), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(empirical_logit = log((successes + .5) / (n - successes + .5)))
p2 <- ggplot(binned, aes(glu, empirical_logit)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(fit)[1], slope = coef(fit)[2], colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Plasma glucose", y = "Binned empirical logit (0.5 correction)")
print(p2)
```

The binned empirical logits use observed outcomes rather than fitted probabilities.
The spline comparison and this descriptive plot can reveal departures from a
linear logit, but a nonsignificant test does not establish that assumption.

## 4. Conduct

```{r}
tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE)
glance(fit)
```

```{r}
pred_prob <- predict(fit, type = "response")
pred_class <- ifelse(pred_prob > 0.5, "Yes", "No")
table(pred_class, truth = pima$type)
```

## 5. Concluding statement

> In `r nrow(pima)` women, each 10 mg/dL increase in plasma glucose
> was associated with an odds ratio for diabetes of
> `r round(exp(10 * coef(fit)["glu"]), 2)` (95% CI from profile:
> `r round(exp(10 * confint(fit)["glu", 1]), 2)` to
> `r round(exp(10 * confint(fit)["glu", 2]), 2)`). At a 0.5 threshold
> the classifier had apparent training-sample
> `r round(100 * mean(pred_class == pima$type), 1)`% accuracy; a
> threshold-free assessment appears in Week 3 Session 5.

::: {.notes}
Most readers prefer ORs reported per 10 units of a continuous predictor
rather than per single unit; the per-unit OR sometimes looks
implausibly close to 1.
:::

## Common pitfalls

- Reporting the coefficient on the log-odds scale without exponentiating.
- Confusing probability and odds.
- Evaluating the model with accuracy at one threshold and nothing else.

## Further reading

- Hosmer DW, Lemeshow S. *Applied Logistic Regression*.
- Harrell FE. *Regression Modeling Strategies*, ch. 10.
- Gelman A, Hill J. *Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel…*.
